extracted.intended_audience: federal judges, patent litigators, and patent counsel preparing or opposing §101 (Alice/Mayo) challenges in software/data-management cases
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and standards for evaluating whether patent claims (particularly software/data-management claims) are directed to patent-eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, including procedural considerations for Rule 12(c) motions and conversion to summary judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patentable subject matter (35 U.S.C. § 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. § 101, patentable subject matter includes 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof.' The provision contains an implicit exception: laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must recognize the implicit exceptions because monopolization of these basic tools might impede innovation. (Alice Corp. cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the patent is directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon. If not, the inquiry ends. Step 2: If it is directed to such an exception, determine whether the claim elements individually and 'as an ordered combination' add an 'inventive concept' that transforms the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims fail to provide an inventive concept at step two, the patent is ineligible. (Alice Corp.; Mayo cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-one focus: look to the claimed advance over the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: At Alice step one, the court looks at 'the focus of the claimed advance over the prior art' to determine whether the claim's character as a whole is directed to excluded subject matter and avoid overgeneralization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful not to overgeneralize claims into high-level abstractions (which would render nearly all inventions 'abstract'), nor to be misled by drafting that attempts to monopolize an abstract idea. (Affinity Labs, Diamond v. Diehr cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Software-specific inquiry: specific asserted improvement vs generic computer implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: In software cases, inquiry often turns on whether claims focus on 'the specific asserted improvement in computer capabilities' or instead on a process that invokes computers merely as a tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claims recite a software-specific improvement (e.g., a new data structure or new way of scanning/attaching security profiles), they are more likely to be non-abstract. Refer to Enfish, Finjan, McRO examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of specific means/method — improved result insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely stating an 'improved result' is insufficient for eligibility; the patent must recite a 'specific means or method that solves a problem in an existing technological process.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that only promise an improved result without specifying how to achieve it are inadequate (Koninklijke KPN v. Gemalto cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purely functional language and conventional technology indicates abstractness
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite only purely functional language and use conventional technology in a typical manner are likely directed to an abstract idea and not eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims risk covering an abstract combination of processes without adding 'any particular assertedly inventive technology.' (Electric Power Group cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that recite mental processes or mathematical algorithms are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely recite steps people go through in their minds, or mathematical algorithms, without more, are treated as abstract mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim elements can be performed mentally or are standard algorithms not tied to a technical improvement, they are likely ineligible. (TLI example cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed subject-matter with fixed parameters required
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility favors claims that define some fixed subject-matter with fixed parameters—i.e., specific steps or structures with defined characteristics—rather than sweeping functional descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents like Finjan and Enfish were non-abstract because they claimed concrete, software-specific structures or steps that improved computer functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: A result alone is not patentable; must claim specific steps to achieve it
rubrics_metrics.description: An innovative result standing alone does not render a claim patentable; the claims must recite the specific steps or means that accomplish that result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look for the particular steps that accomplish an improvement; bare recitation of the result is insufficient (Finjan cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption is the central concern in Alice/Mayo
rubrics_metrics.description: Preventing preemption of fundamental building blocks (abstract ideas, laws of nature) is central to the Alice/Mayo analysis; claims that would effectively monopolize an abstract idea weigh against eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis should ensure claims do not foreclose future innovation by broadly preempting use of an abstract idea or basic tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(c) motion standard for judgment on the pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Rule 12(c) motion challenges the sufficiency of the complaint after an answer has been filed; the standard is functionally identical to a motion to dismiss. Disputed material facts preclude judgment on the pleadings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may consider pleadings, documents incorporated by reference, and matters of judicial notice when deciding such a motion. (Hal Roach, Heliotrope Gen. citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion to summary judgment — notice and evidence considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting a Rule 12(c) motion into one for summary judgment is generally inappropriate where only the nonmoving party has introduced evidentiary exhibits in response; courts should give parties notice of intent to convert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conversion without notice or when only the nonmovant has submitted evidence is improper; timeliness and fairness concerns also factor into conversion decisions. (Two-Way Media, James cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction definitions (Judge Davis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Court's claim constructions: (1) 'Data items' = 'sequence of bits'; (2) 'Data files' = 'a named data item(s)'; (3) 'Substantially unique identifier, Data identifier, True Name, Digital identifier, Data item identifier' = 'an identity for a data item generated by processing all of the data in the data item, and only the data in the data item, through an algorithm that makes the identifier substantially unique.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructions guide how the asserted claims are interpreted in eligibility and validity analyses; precise construction can affect novelty and eligibility outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102: prior art showing same hash-based content identifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are anticipated (not novel) if prior art discloses using content-based identifiers, calculated from the contents of a data item via hash/message-digest functions, to perform the same data-management tasks claimed (detecting duplicates, accessing files, comparing identifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB found multiple claims invalid as anticipated by prior art (e.g., Woodhill, Kantor, Langer) where prior systems used hash-based binary object identifiers that changed when contents changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hash vs. message digest equivalence (technical note)
rubrics_metrics.description: The True Name patents use the terms 'hash' and 'message digest' interchangeably; 'message digest' functions (like MD5) are a type of hash function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence matters when construing claims that refer to 'hash' or 'message digest' functions and when comparing to prior-art disclosures that may use differing terminology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty nuance: one-to-one comparison vs comparing to a plurality (PersonalWeb)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art system that inherently discloses only one-to-one comparisons of content-based identifiers does not necessarily anticipate a claim that requires comparing a content-based identifier with a plurality of identifiers; this distinction can support novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit reversed PTAB where prior art did not inherently disclose comparing one identifier against multiple identifiers (PersonalWeb v. Apple). Careful parsing of prior-art capabilities vs claimed features is required.
